label: D2 after choosing a2 and landing rarely in S1 (a2 -> S1 rare transition)
explanation: Fires only at D2, exactly when the last-action input is a2 and the state input is S1, i.e. the rare transition from a2. Uses observed inputs only (equivalent to action==2 & state==1 at D2). Dev: precision 1.0, recall 0.995, mass recall 0.9998. Never fires at D1 or GO, on a1->S1 common, a2->S2 common or a1->S2 rare. The ~300 misses are tiny activations (<=0.12 of max) mostly on a1->S1 or a2->S2 D2 steps. Activation is near-constant (median 3.73, max 4.55); I did not verify what modulates the small magnitude variation.

issues: No refutation found. Test split: precision 1.0, recall 0.994, F1 0.997, mass recall 0.9998, correlation 0.99. There are 0 false positives.
The claim 'never fires at D1 or GO' holds: on test, phase==D1 and phase==GO each have precision 0 and recall 0. On dev, every activation is at D2.
The other three transitions barely fire. On test, precision is 0.0017 for a1->S1, 0.0 for a1->S2 and 0.0007 for a2->S2. So the feature is specific to a2->S1, not to rare transitions in general.

The 340 missed steps on test carry 0.0% of the activation mass. They are tiny activations of about 0.01-0.02 of max, scattered over common D2 steps (a2->S2, a1->S1). They show no pattern by trial position, reward or good state.

Minor: the D2 step is not observed-only in the strict sense. 'common' is a future variable before D2, but at D2 the reached state is an input, so (action==2)&(state==1) is the same as (action==2)&(common==0). The scores are identical. The predicate uses in_action and in_state, which are observed, so it is fine.
Not checked, as the original author also said: what drives the small magnitude variation (median 3.73, max 4.55).
